## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll read the last two reviews, retain the 20k opponent, and play game 152 to completion. I’ll focus on securing broad eye space early and save the full game and lessons for the next session.

## Connections improved locally; width was insufficient

C4/G3 began two lower bases. White G7/C7 took both upper corners.
E4 extended the lower boundary and White E5 capped it.
D4 immediately joined C4/E4, avoiding the delayed two-junction left connection failure of150.

total38.

The count was made at the required early stage, but the response did not produce enough viable width.

F3 joined G3, then E3 actually joined F3 to E4/main.

J4/A5 and the lower boundaries remained open: do not treat37 as secure final area.
White C6 capped C5, Black B5 joined C5, and White B6 closed upward left expansion.

All nine final lower Black stones remained in one chain.
Timely orthogonal joins were a local improvement, but a connected narrow outline still lacked winning territory.
Neither this game nor the prior wins establish an optimal opening or individual move values.
The useful strategic requirement is to plan sufficient viable room alongside connections, rather than spend the opening joining an already undersized outline.

## Late central entry had no completed room

Black19 E7 entered a separate chain between White C7/G7/E5.
Its current liberties E6/D7/F7/E8 were routes, not eye space.
White20 E8 occupied the direct upper route immediately.
This first cap should have triggered a concrete room audit: no enclosed upper base existed, and escaping through a neighboring junction required further turns.

D7 at21 actually joined E7, but White D8 capped the upper-left route.
E6 at23 joined downward and pressed White D5/E5.
An informal central capture hope depended on preventing those stones from connecting.
Actual White24 F5 joined D5/E5 to F4/G5. That capture hope was invalidated; it was not an isolated enemy target.

F6 at25 joined E6 and aimed toward G6.
White26 G6 actually joined G5/G7 and blocked the right escape.
F7 at27 joined both E7/F6, but White28 F8 joined E8/D8 and closed the upper escape.
Thus every Black extension was physically connected, yet none created eye room or reached a viable base.

The result reinforces the distinction between connection and life.
The first cap, E8, was the earlier decision point; waiting until the final liberty was gone added four stones to a roomless entry.
No unplayed alternative is established as forced-safe or winning.

## Exact final-liberty audit and resignation

Upper Black five: D7/E6/E7/F6/F7, sole liberty D6.
At D6 the orthogonal neighbors are White C6/D5 and Black D7/E6.
Filling D6 would join the upper chain but leave it with no liberty.

Adjacent White left chain B6/C6/C7 has A6/B7/C8/D6.
Adjacent White central chain D5/E5/F4/F5/G5/G6/G7 has D6/G4/G8/H5/H6/H7.
Both retain other liberties after Black D6, so neither would be captured.
Black D6 is therefore suicide, not a legal extension, an eye, or a capture-of-attacker defense.
It was not submitted. No invalid move occurred.

Black resigned with the upper entry unsavable by direct extension and no sufficient additional room established.
This is a practical resignation judgment, not a proof of every possible whole-board continuation or a numerical final margin.

The lower chain had ten liberties but no completed unconditional two-eye proof.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.

1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
